name: Alabama white sauce wings
aliases: white barbecue sauce wings|white sauce wings|Decatur-style
what: Wings smoked over hickory and then coated or dunked in white sauce — a mayonnaise-based barbecue sauce with vinegar, lemon juice, black pepper, salt, and in many versions cayenne and horseradish. It is thin, sharp and pale, and it goes on at the end of the cook rather than during it, because mayonnaise breaks over heat. The result is tangy rather than sweet, with none of the tomato or molasses a reader expects from the word barbecue.

name: Lemon pepper wings
aliases: lemon pepper dry|lemon pepper wet|LP wings
what: A wing cooked without breading and finished in lemon pepper — granulated lemon zest mashed with cracked black pepper, then baked and dried, usually with salt and sugar in the blend. Atlanta orders it two ways. Dry means the seasoning goes on alone. Wet means a sauce underneath it, butter or a lemon sauce or Buffalo, with the dry seasoning shaken over the top. The wing plate comes with fried rice at a great many Atlanta counters, and Wikipedia calls the dish emblematic of the city's cuisine.

name: Old Bay wings
what: A wing finished in Old Bay — a blend of eighteen herbs and spices built in Baltimore in 1939, celery salt first, with red and black pepper and paprika, and bay leaves, mustard, cardamom, cloves and ginger among the rest. It goes on dry out of the fryer, or in butter as a wet toss, and it is the same can that goes on steamed blue crab, on fries, on popcorn and around the rim of a beer glass. Salt and celery seed do the work, not heat; a customer who wants heat adds hot sauce on top.

name: Buffalo wings
what: A chicken wing cut into a drumette and a flat, deep-fried bare — no batter, no flour — then shaken in a bowl with melted butter and a vinegar-based cayenne pepper sauce, and served hot with celery, carrot sticks and a dip of blue cheese or ranch. Heat runs mild, medium and hot, and the order names the heat before it names the count. The wing is named for Buffalo, New York, and has nothing to do with the animal.

name: Jerk wings
what: Wings dry-rubbed or wet-marinated in Jamaican jerk seasoning and cooked over fire until the outside blackens. Allspice and Scotch bonnet peppers carry it; cloves, cinnamon, scallions, nutmeg, thyme, garlic, brown sugar, ginger, soy sauce, vinegar and salt fill it out. The seasoning goes on before the heat, which is the whole difference from a wing that gets sauced after the fryer. Smoke comes from the fuel — pimento wood traditionally, charcoal in a split oil drum in most places that sell it — and the finish is char, not gloss. A scotch-bonnet sauce goes on afterward at the counter's discretion.

name: Chicago mild sauce wings
aliases: mild sauce wings|South Side wings|fried hard with mild
what: Wings fried hard — left in the oil past golden until the skin goes dark and brittle — then handed over a counter in a box with french fries and a slice of white bread, the whole box doused in mild sauce. Mild sauce is a tomato condiment of Chicago's Black South and West Sides: ketchup and tomato paste with sugar, vinegar and spices, pungent and sweet with a vinegar sting. It is a pour, not a toss. The sauce goes over everything in the box, and the bread and the fries take as much of it as the wings do.

name: Mumbo sauce wings
aliases: mambo sauce wings|wings and mumbo|carryout wings
what: Fried chicken wings, usually whole and uncut, sold through the window of a Washington carryout and drowned in mumbo sauce — red, sweeter than barbecue sauce and by turns sharper or more sour, depending whose kitchen made it. The same sauce goes on french fries, fried jumbo shrimp and fried rice, and the wings-over-fried-rice box is the form the dish most often takes across the D.C., Maryland and Virginia carryouts. The sauce arrives poured, not tossed, and the container it comes in is styrofoam.

name: Garlic parmesan wings
what: A fried wing tossed in melted butter or oil with garlic and grated parmesan, often with dried herbs and black pepper, sometimes finished with more cheese out of the bowl so it sits in visible flecks. It carries no chile heat, which is the point: it is the order placed by the person at the table who does not want heat, and it sells beside Buffalo rather than against it. Some kitchens pour it as a sauce, some dust dry cheese onto a buttered wing, and the two versions eat differently — one slick, one powdery.

name: Korean fried chicken wings
aliases: KFC (Korean fried chicken)|yangnyeom wings|soy garlic wings|chikin
what: Chicken fried twice so the crust comes out thin and brittle — Julia Moskin of The New York Times called it "thin, crackly and almost transparent" — then hand-painted with sauce by brush rather than shaken in a bowl, so the coating stays a thin film and the crust keeps its snap. Two sauces carry the style: yangnyeom, sweet and spicy on a gochujang base, and ganjang, soy and sugar and a great deal of garlic. Wings and drums arrive whole or jointed depending on the house. Pickled radish comes in a tub alongside, and beer with it; the pairing has its own word, chimaek, from chicken and maekju.

name: Memphis dry-rub wings
what: A wing finished with the rub that Memphis puts on ribs — salt and a spice blend, house by house, usually paprika-led — and handed over without sauce. The city's rib counters run the dry-and-wet split: dry means rubbed before cooking and eaten as is, wet means brushed with sauce before, during and after. The wing borrows the split whole. It comes off a smoker at some houses, out of a fryer at others, and off both at a few, and the rub goes on at the end either way so the seasoning stays granular instead of dissolving.

name: Nashville hot wings
aliases: hot chicken wings|hot wings, Nashville style
what: Hot chicken's method put on a wing: marinate in a water- or buttermilk-based seasoned blend, flour, fry, then paint with a cayenne paste loosened with fat drawn from the fryer. The paste stains the crust deep red and goes on with a spoon and gloved hands, then gets squeezed in. It lands on white bread with pickle chips — the bread catching the grease, the pickles cutting it — and the bread is part of the dish, not a napkin. Heat runs in named steps and the top step is genuinely punishing.

name: Rochester breaded wings
what: A chicken wing dredged in seasoned flour before it goes in the oil, fried until the coating sets hard, then glazed rather than tossed loose — most often in Country Sweet, a sweet-and-tangy sauce a Rochester kitchen built in 1977 that is neither barbecue nor cayenne-and-butter. Breading is the whole argument: seventy miles west, Buffalo puts the wing in the fryer bare. Rochester bars also pour plain cayenne sauce, barbecue, teriyaki and garlic parmesan, so a breaded wing is a coating rather than a single flavour.

name: Smoked barbecue wings
what: A wing cooked on a barbecue pit rather than in oil: rubbed, smoked over wood until the fat renders, then finished — brushed with a tomato sauce and set over higher heat to tack up, or dropped briefly in the fryer so the skin crisps. Regional sauce follows regional pit. Kansas City runs thick tomato sauces; Memphis runs the dry-and-wet split; Texas leans on the rub and the wood. The wing is a side item on those menus, cooked with the ribs and the shoulder and sold beside them.

name: Alabama white sauce
what: A mayonnaise-based barbecue sauce, thin, pale and sharp. Typical ingredients are vinegar, lemon juice, salt, pepper, cayenne pepper and horseradish stirred into mayonnaise. It goes on barbecue chicken, which is an Alabama speciality, and on wings — dunked whole rather than brushed.

name: Blue cheese dressing
what: A thick white dip of blue cheese with mayonnaise and buttermilk, sour cream or yogurt, plus milk, vinegar, onion powder and garlic powder. A vinaigrette version exists — salad oil, blue cheese, vinegar and seasonings — and is not what comes with wings. Sold by most major dressing makers in the United States and Canada, and served as the dip beside Buffalo wings and raw vegetables.

name: Buffalo sauce
what: Cayenne pepper hot sauce cut with melted butter. Two things, warmed together and held warm, poured over fried wings in a metal bowl and shaken. More butter reads mild, less reads hot, and a kitchen moves between the three by changing that ratio rather than the pepper. Worcestershire sauce and garlic powder turn up in plenty of versions. Bottled ready-to-use wing sauce does the same job with oil and butter flavouring in place of butter, because butter separates on a shelf.

name: Crystal Hot Sauce
what: A reddish-orange Louisiana pepper sauce made by Baumer Foods since 1923: aged red cayenne peppers, distilled vinegar, salt. Three ingredients on the 6 fl oz bottle; the gallon jug adds xanthan gum. Writers put it against Tabasco as having "a more prominent dark chile flavor, and a slightly subdued vinegar profile". Buffalo kitchens that do not buy Frank's usually buy this.

name: Frank's RedHot
aliases: Frank's|Frank's RedHot Original Cayenne Pepper Sauce
what: A thin orange cayenne pepper sauce: aged cayenne red peppers, distilled vinegar, water, salt, garlic powder, in that order on the label. McCormick & Company makes it. The Original blend measures 450 Scoville heat units — the capsaicin scale named for Wilbur Scoville — which puts it below Tabasco, Cholula and Tapatío, and barely above Sriracha; the XTRA Hot blend measures 2,000. It is the bottle most Buffalo wing recipes start from.

name: Garlic parmesan sauce
what: A pale, garlicky wing coating with parmesan in it. Two versions share the name: a creamy emulsified sauce built on oil and egg yolk with parmesan powder, sold bottled; and a kitchen mix of melted butter, minced garlic and grated parmesan tossed over the wings and finished with more cheese and parsley. Neither has heat in it. Both leave the wing wet and the fingers cheesy.

name: Honey barbecue sauce
what: A thick sweet red sauce: corn syrup or sugar, vinegar, tomato, honey, smoke flavour and spices. Sticky enough to hold on a wing without butter, sweet enough to caramelise under a broiler or on a grill. Every wing chain sells one, and it is usually the mildest thing on the board.

name: Hot honey
what: Honey with chillies in it. Sweet first, then a heat that builds slowly — the flavour writers describe as "sweet-first" with a "slow-building heat". Goes on pizza, on fried chicken and wings, on roasted vegetables, with cheese, in sandwiches, on desserts, into glazes and marinades and dipping sauces, and into mixed drinks.

name: Jerk marinade
what: A wet marinade, or a dry rub, built on allspice and Scotch bonnet peppers — both native to Jamaica and grown there by the Taíno. Scallion, thyme, garlic, ginger, cloves, cinnamon, nutmeg, brown sugar, soy sauce, vinegar and salt turn up in it. The heat is the Scotch bonnet's. The word 'jerk' names the rub, the marinade and mop sauce made from it, and the cooking technique, all three.

name: Lemon pepper
what: A dry blend of granulated lemon zest and cracked black peppercorns. The zest is mashed into the pepper so citrus oil soaks in, then the mix is baked and dried. Commercial blends add salt, sugar, onion powder, garlic powder, citric acid, lemon flavouring, sometimes cayenne. It started as a seafood seasoning and became the wing seasoning Atlanta is known for.

name: Lemon pepper wet
what: A wing that has been through something wet and then through lemon pepper. The wet part varies: a lemon sauce instead of a dry rub at some shops, melted butter at others, Buffalo sauce at others again, with the dry seasoning shaken on after. American Deli in Atlanta invented the version the name usually points at.

name: Mango habanero
what: A sweet-then-hot wing sauce: mango purée and corn syrup in front, habanero and cayenne behind. Orange, thick, and built to be tossed. It is the standard second-from-the-top rung on a chain wing board — hot enough to be a choice, sweet enough to finish.

name: Memphis dry rub
what: A dry mix of salt, paprika, sugar and spices, patted onto meat before it cooks and shaken over it again after. Memphis barbecue is mostly pork — ribs and shoulders — and its ribs come dry or wet: dry means rub and no sauce, wet means sauce brushed on before, during and after. The same rub goes on wings, which get the rib counter's treatment without the pit.

name: Mild sauce
what: A red-brown condiment poured over fried chicken and wings on Chicago's South and West Sides. Recipes vary a great deal; many versions combine ketchup, barbecue sauce and hot sauce. Close kin to barbecue sauce and to mumbo sauce, and particularly associated with Black communities in Chicago. The name is not a heat rating — it is what the sauce is called.

name: Mumbo sauce
what: A carryout condiment of Washington, D.C.: red-orange, thick, poured over fried chicken wings, french fries, fried jumbo shrimp and fried rice. Close to barbecue sauce but sweeter, and either spicier or more sour depending on whose it is. The consistency and the flavour vary shop to shop. Its origin and its ingredients are both disputed, and so is its spelling.

name: Nashville hot paste
what: A cayenne paste, spooned onto fried chicken the moment it leaves the fryer. Fat carries it — lard or a ladle of the frying oil itself — which is why it soaks in rather than sitting on top, and why the bird turns deep red. Some shops add sugar, garlic or extra hot sauce. Some apply it before breading instead of after. Recipes are kept close.

name: Old Bay Seasoning
what: A blend of eighteen herbs and spices built on celery salt — salt and celery seed — with red pepper, black pepper and paprika. Bay leaves, mustard, cardamom, cloves and ginger are among the others listed for the original product held at the Baltimore Museum of Industry. Made for crab and shrimp; used on wings, fries, popcorn, eggs, corn and a great deal else across Maryland, Virginia and the rest of the Mid-Atlantic.

name: Ranch dressing
what: A savoury creamy dressing of buttermilk, salt, garlic, onion, black pepper and herbs — commonly chives, parsley and dill — mixed into mayonnaise or another oil emulsion. Sour cream and yogurt sometimes stand in for the buttermilk or the mayonnaise. It has been the best-selling salad dressing in the United States since 1992, when it passed Italian, and it is the most popular wing dip in the country.

name: Soy garlic sauce
what: A brown glaze of soy sauce, sugar and garlic, brushed onto fried chicken after the fryer. Sweet and savoury rather than hot; often heavily garlicky. Ganjang-chikin — soy sauce chicken — is the Korean name for the dish it makes. A honey version, sweeter and stickier, is sold alongside it.

name: Sweet chili sauce
aliases: sweet Thai chili sauce|nam chim kai|น้ำจิ้มไก่
what: A clear, thickened red sauce of chillies, rice wine vinegar and sugar, often with garlic and sometimes fish sauce. Red chilli peppers — Fresno, Thai or red jalapeños — give it its flecks. Known in Thailand as nam chim kai, a dipping sauce for chicken, and used across Thai, Afghan, Malaysian and Western cooking. In European Chinese restaurants it is the dip for prawn toast, egg rolls, lettuce wraps, spring rolls and chicken wings.

name: Teriyaki sauce
what: Soy sauce, mirin or sake, and sugar, boiled down to a glaze. The Japanese name for it is tare (タレ). Traditionally the meat is dipped in it or brushed with it while cooking; ginger goes in sometimes, spring onion over the top. In North America the word covers any dish made with a teriyaki-like sauce, including versions using substitutes for sake or mirin, or adding sesame or garlic — both uncommon in Japanese cooking. It goes on chicken wings and is used as a dipping sauce.

name: Yangnyeom sauce
what: A sweet and spicy glaze built on gochujang — a fermented Korean paste of red chili powder, glutinous rice, fermented soybean powder, barley malt powder and salt — with garlic, sugar and other seasonings. Painted onto fried chicken with a brush after the fryer, in a thin even coat rather than a toss. Yangnyeom chicken is the dish; this is what makes it.

name: beef on weck
what: Rare roast beef, hand-carved thin, on a kummelweck roll topped with kosher salt and caraway seeds. The cut face of the top half gets dipped in jus from the roast; prepared horseradish comes on the side for the eater to spread. Along with wings and sponge candy it is one of the three best-known Buffalo specialties.

name: boneless wings
what: Small pieces of skinless, boneless chicken breast coated in flour and spices, then fried or baked, like a chicken nugget, and tossed in or served with the same sauces as a Buffalo wing. Restaurants began offering them after the price of raw wings rose and as some diners wanted a neater way to eat; they are sometimes marketed under the name wyngz.

name: buffalo chicken dip
what: Shredded chicken, cream cheese, cayenne-and-butter wing sauce and a dairy dressing, baked until it bubbles and eaten hot with chips, celery or bread. It takes the flavour of a wing and removes the bone, the skin, the fryer and the plate.

name: buffalo chicken pizza
what: A pizza sauced with cayenne-and-butter wing sauce instead of tomato, topped with chicken and mozzarella, and finished with blue cheese or ranch. Buffalo is applied here to a dish that is seasoned with the sauce rather than fried in the style at all.

name: celery and carrots
what: Cut celery, usually with carrot sticks, served cold beside hot wings with a cup of blue cheese or ranch that both the vegetables and the wings go into. Celery here is the petiole — the leaf stalk of Apium graveolens — cut raw to finger length. It cools the mouth between wings, it carries dip, and it is the one item on the plate nobody asks for.

name: chicken and waffles
what: Fried chicken on a waffle, eaten with butter and syrup as a waffle would be, and often with hot sauce. It belongs to several culinary traditions at once — Pennsylvania Dutch cuisine and soul food among them — and the two versions are not the same dish.

name: chicken riggies
what: An Italian-American pasta dish from the Utica–Rome area of New York: chicken, rigatoni, and hot or sweet peppers in a spicy cream-and-tomato sauce. Variations are many; the peppers and the rigatoni are the constants.

name: french fries
what: Potatoes cut into even batonnet or julienne strips, dried, and deep-fried. Beside wings they do three jobs: they soak the sauce that drips, they stretch a small order into a meal, and in several cities they become the plate the wings sit on.

name: the fried rice plate
aliases: wings over fried rice|wings and rice
what: Whole fried chicken wings served over egg fried rice with mumbo sauce, sold from Chinese-American carryouts across the Washington, D.C. metropolitan region. The wings are not cut; they go into the oil whole and come out as a set of three-jointed pieces laid over the rice.

name: Garbage Plate
what: Hot dog or hamburger meat and a meat hot sauce piled on a bed of side dishes — usually macaroni salad and home fries — with onions and mustard, and buttered bread alongside. Rochester's signature dish, and a trademark of one restaurant that every other restaurant has to work around.

name: jojo potatoes
what: A potato wedge that has been breaded, pressure-fried and spiced — not a bare wedge, and not a fry. The pressure fryer is a pressure cooker filled with hot oil, so the potato cooks fast and hard while keeping its water. Sold beside fried chicken across the Pacific Northwest, and in pockets of Montana, Minnesota, Nebraska, Northeast Ohio and upstate New York.

name: mozzarella sticks
what: Elongated pieces of mozzarella coated in breadcrumbs or batter and fried, served as an hors d'oeuvre with marinara. On a wing menu they are the thing a table orders when half of it does not want wings.

name: mumbo fries
what: French fries under mumbo sauce, from a Washington, D.C. carryout. Mumbo is a sweet, tangy, ketchup-based condiment — like barbecue sauce but sweeter, and somewhat spicier or more sour, with real variation in flavour and consistency between makers.

name: pickled radish
what: Cubed pickled daikon in a sweet-sour brine, served cold in a small tub beside Korean fried chicken. Pickled radishes and beer or carbonated drinks are the standard accompaniment; Bonchon lists pickled radish among its side dishes alongside kimchi, coleslaw and Korean street corn.

name: pizza logs
what: Mozzarella, and often pepperoni, rolled in an egg-roll wrapper and deep-fried, served with marinara to dip. A Western New York bar snack that sits on the same appetizer list as wings and sells in freezer cases across upstate.

name: the pitcher
what: Draught beer sold by the jug for a table to share. It is the other half of a wing order almost everywhere wings are sold, and in two traditions it is named into the food: Hooters built its concept on wings and beer, and Korean has a single word for the pairing.

name: white bread and pickles
what: Two slices of plain white sandwich bread with pickle chips on top, and the hot chicken laid over both. The bread catches the cayenne paste and the fat coming off the bird; the pickles cut it. It is not a side — it is the plate.

name: the wing basket
aliases: a basket of wings|wing order|the plate
what: The unit a bar sells wings in: a count of pieces in a basket or on a plate, lined with paper, with celery and carrots, a cup of blue cheese or ranch, and usually fries. A fry basket is the tool the wings come out of the oil in — it contains the food in the fryer and strains it on the way out — and the serving basket copies its shape.

name: the air fryer
what: A small countertop convection oven that reaches deep-frying temperatures without submerging the food in oil. It circulates air at up to 200 °C / 392 °F to brown food coated in a thin layer of oil, where conventional frying drives the same browning reactions at 140–165 °C / 284–329 °F by putting the food in hot oil instead. Food sits in a basket over a drip tray, and for small pieces the basket must be shaken.

name: the baking powder bake
what: The home method that gets wing skin to crisp in an oven: toss dried wings with baking powder and salt, bake low to render and dry, then hot to brown. No fryer, no pot of oil, and a crust that holds sauce for about as long as it takes to eat.

name: the breaded fry
what: Coating a wing before it goes in the oil — flour, seasoned flour, batter or crumbs — so the crust rather than the skin carries the crunch and holds the sauce. One common method for preparing food for deep frying involves adding multiple layers of batter around the food, such as cornmeal, flour or tempura; breadcrumbs may also be used.

name: the brine
what: Salting the bird before it cooks. Brining treats food with brine or coarse salt, which preserves and seasons it while enhancing tenderness. A wet brine immerses the meat in salt water; a dry brine covers it in coarse salt, which draws moisture out of the interior to the surface where it mixes with the salt and is then reabsorbed.

name: the deep fryer
what: The machine or pot the wing goes into: food submerged in hot fat rather than shallow-fried in a pan. A commercial vat, a chip pan, a wok, a Dutch oven or a cast-iron pot all do it. Industrially, a pressure fryer or a vacuum fryer may be used. Fry baskets contain the food in the fryer and strain it on the way out, and a thermometer is the other tool that matters.

name: the double fry
what: Frying in two passes with a rest between them. The first pass cooks the piece through and drives water out of the skin; the rest lets the surface dry and the interior even out; the second pass, hotter, builds the crust. The result is the thin, hard, glassy shell that will not go soft under sauce.

name: the dredge
what: Coating food before it fries. One common method for preparing food for deep frying involves adding multiple layers of batter around the food — cornmeal, flour or tempura — and breadcrumbs may be used. On a wing it is the difference between Buffalo and Rochester; on everything else at the counter it is simply how the thing is made.

name: frying oil
what: What the wing is cooked in. Deep frying submerges food in hot fat — traditionally lard, today most commonly oil — and the choice of fat sets flavour, how long the vat lasts, what the shop pays and what goes on the allergen sheet. Four answers cover most American wing counters: beef tallow, peanut, soybean and canola.

name: the grill
what: Cooking the wing over direct heat instead of in oil. Buffalo's own reference text lists it among the alternatives — traditionally deep-fried, but alternatively baked, grilled, or broiled — and the Anchor Bar's account rules it out for its own wings: they are not grilled, but only deep-fried and slightly crispy.

name: the naked fry
what: Frying a wing with nothing on it — no batter, no flour, no crumb. The skin browns and crisps on its own, the fat under it renders into the oil, and the sauce goes on afterwards. A Buffalo wing is an unbreaded chicken wing section, deep-fried and then coated or dipped in cayenne sauce and melted butter.

name: the par-cook
what: Cooking the wing most of the way in advance and finishing it to order. The first pass drives out water and cooks the meat through; the finishing pass, hotter and short, browns it. It is the same architecture as a double fry, separated by hours instead of minutes and done for service rather than for texture.

name: sauce on the side
aliases: on the side|naked with sauce|dry with a cup
what: Ordering the wings unsauced with the sauce in a cup. The argument is whether the sauce is a step in the cooking or a condiment at the table — and the traditions answer it differently, on the record, in their own methods.

name: smoke then fry
what: Cooking the wing through in smoke, then dropping it briefly into hot oil or onto high heat to tighten the skin. Smoke gives flavour and colour that a fryer cannot; the fryer gives a crust that smoke alone leaves flabby. The rub or the sauce goes on after.

name: the toss
what: The metal bowl. Cooked wings go into a bowl or pot, sauce goes over them, and the whole thing is shaken to coat the wings completely before serving. It is the last step of a Buffalo wing and the only one that touches the wing after the oil.

name: the wing cut
aliases: breaking down a wing|segmenting|jointing the wing
what: Where the knife goes on a chicken wing. The wing comes off the bird in three segments and the cook cuts it at both joints: the drumette, shaped like a small drumstick and white meat; the middle flat, also called the wingette, containing two bones; and the tip, often discarded or used for stock. Two pieces go in the basket, so one wing off the bird sells as two wings on a menu.

name: American Deli
what: A counter chain out of Atlanta, open since 1989, that sells wings by the ten-piece with a long board of seasonings and sauces. Lemon pepper wet — wings sauced and then hit with dry lemon pepper — was invented here, and the company now runs more than 200 stores across ten states.

name: Anchor Bar
aliases: Anchor Bar Buffalo|Frank & Teressa's Anchor Bar
what: A bar and restaurant at Main and North in Buffalo, open since 1935, which claims the Buffalo wing and has trademarked the phrase. Frank and Teressa Bellissimo opened it; their son Dominic ran it and sold the story. The dining room keeps the motorcycles, the jukebox and the original bar, and the wings go out bare-fried with blue cheese and celery.

name: Atomic Wings
what: A New York wing chain founded in 1989 by a man trying to reproduce what he had eaten as a student in Buffalo. Wings are cut by hand and breaded on the premises, which is not the Buffalo method, and sauced from more than a dozen house mixes. Shops are small — 800 to 1,500 square feet — and built for takeout rather than for sitting.

name: Bar-Bill Tavern
what: A tavern on Main Street in East Aurora, fifteen miles southeast of Buffalo and not in the city at all, whose wings are brushed with sauce by hand rather than tossed. An order comes as five drums and five flats around a bowl of blue cheese made on the premises. Beef on weck comes off the same kitchen, carved to order.

name: Big Bob Gibson Bar-B-Q
aliases: Big Bob Gibson's Bar-B-Q|Big Bob Gibson
what: The Decatur, Alabama pit where white barbecue sauce was invented: mayonnaise, vinegar and black pepper, made for smoked chicken. Bob Gibson started it in 1925; four generations of his family have run it since, and its competition team won first place for smoked wings at Memphis in May in 2021.

name: Blondies Sports
what: A sports bar on West 79th Street between Amsterdam and Broadway, on Manhattan's Upper West Side, with televisions in every sightline and a wing order most of the room is there for. NYC Tourism calls it "a female-owned fixture on the Upper West Side for more than 35 years." It runs late — later than almost any wing room in this set.

name: Bolton's Spicy Chicken & Fish
what: A small East Nashville counter at 624 Main Street selling spicy fried chicken and spicy fried fish, opened in 1997 by Bolton Matthews and Dolly Ingram. The recipe came down from Matthews's uncle Bolton Polk. Its heat is the reference point other Nashville houses get measured by.

name: Bonchon
what: A Korean fried chicken chain that fries each piece twice and paints the sauce on with a brush. Jinduk Seo opened the first Bonchon in Busan, South Korea in 2002; the company now runs about 500 restaurants in more than ten countries and territories, keeps its global headquarters in Dallas, and manufactures every sauce in South Korea. Two sauces carry the brand: soy garlic and spicy. The chain closed its own South Korean restaurants at the end of 2016 and has exported ever since.

name: Buffalo Wild Wings
what: A sports-bar chain that put a Buffalo wing on a menu in Columbus, Ohio in 1982 and then on menus in all fifty states. Jim Disbrow and Scott Lowery opened it beside Ohio State University after failing to find Buffalo-style wings in Ohio. Wings go out in a long list of sauces and dry rubs — the chain's own sauce page counted 26 of them on 16 September 2026 — and the room is built around televised sport. Inspire Brands has owned it since 2018 and runs it from a support center in Sandy Springs, Georgia, which takes an Atlanta mailing address.

name: Capital City Mambo Sauce
what: A bottler, not a counter. Arsha and Charles Jones started Capital City in a home kitchen in 2011 to put D.C. mambo sauce in a jar, and the company now runs a headquarters and distribution building at Melford Town Center in Bowie, Maryland. The bottles reach Giant, Safeway, Wegmans and Target.

name: Central BBQ
what: A Memphis barbecue house started in 2002 by two competition cooks, Craig Blondis and Roger Sapp, on Central Avenue. Smoked hot wings come off the same pit as the ribs, whole, in six finishes: wet, naked, jerked, dry spice, honey gold or sweet heat. The house line is "Smoke is Our Sauce."

name: Chickie's & Pete's
what: A Philadelphia sports bar and crab house that began as a Mayfair taproom in 1977 and now runs stadium, casino and airport rooms. Crabfries are what it is known for; Chickie's Wings come classic in six or ten, boneless in eight or twelve, in buffalo, sweet heat, dry rub or barbecue, with celery and blue cheese or ranch.

name: Ching's Hot Wings
what: A Memphis wing shop on Getwell Road, trading since 2003, selling whole wings by the piece from three to four hundred. Flavours run dry — Seasoned, Lemon Pepper, Dry Hot — and wet, through honey gold, hot, extra hot and one called Suicide. The house combination is the Kam Special: three dry seasonings with a honey hot drizzle over the top.

name: Country Sweet Chicken & Ribs
what: A Rochester counter open since 1977, hand-breading its wings and glazing them in a sauce the founder built in a home kitchen and the city now buys by the bottle. The house says the sauce is "not quite BBQ, and it certainly wasn't Buffalo—it was something entirely new," which is the whole of Rochester's case against Buffalo in one line of its own marketing.

name: Duff's Famous Wings
what: A wing house at Sheridan Drive and Millersport Highway in Amherst, north of Buffalo, open under that corner since 1946 and selling wings since 1969. Eight heat levels run from mild to death, and the house warns at every level that its scale runs hotter than the word suggests. Buffalo's long argument over who started the wing puts Duff's on the other side of it from the Anchor Bar.

name: Elmo's Bar & Restaurant
what: A pitcher-and-television sports bar on Millersport Highway in Getzville, near the University at Buffalo's north campus, whose signature is a wing that goes through the fryer and then onto a grill. The Infatuation calls it the double dip. Orders arrive as sauce combinations — hot and barbecue, cajun and honey mustard — rather than a single heat.

name: Gabriel's Gate
what: A restaurant and tavern at 145 Allen Street in Buffalo's Allentown, trading since 1969 inside an 1864 brick row house with tin ceilings and two wood-burning fireplaces. Wings go out big and crispy, sauced with Frank's RedHot, at heats the house runs "from mild to suicide-hot." Bon Appétit put them first in Buffalo in 2018, which is how a corner restaurant on a bar street acquired a line at the door.

name: Harold's Chicken Shack
aliases: Harold's Chicken|Harold's|Harold's: The Fried Chicken King
what: A Chicago fried-chicken institution founded by Harold Pierce in 1950 and franchised to friends and family, now past a hundred storefronts. The constants across the shops are the chicken dinners and the emblem of a cook chasing a chicken with a cleaver, often crowned; everything else — technique, seasoning, menu — varies shop to shop. The counter question is mild sauce or hot.

name: Hattie B's Hot Chicken
what: A Nashville hot chicken house founded by a father and son both named Nick Bishop, open in Midtown since 2012 and now in seven cities. It is the one with a printed heat ladder, from Southern (no heat) up to Shut the Cluck Up, and it is where most people outside Nashville meet the dish.

name: Hooters
what: A restaurant chain that sells breaded wings, beer and a uniform. Six Clearwater, Florida businessmen incorporated Hooters, Inc. on 1 April 1983 and opened the first restaurant on 4 October that year at 2800 Gulf to Bay Boulevard, in a failed nightclub they bought cheap. Waiting staff are young women in a branded tank top and orange running shorts, called Hooters Girls, and the company has defended that hiring in court for thirty years. The wings come four ways: hand-breaded, naked, grilled in Daytona Beach sauce, or boneless.

name: Horace & Dickie's Seafood
what: A fried-fish carryout that ran thirty years at 12th and H Streets NE in Washington and now trades from Prince George's County, Maryland. Whiting on white or brown bread is the order it is known for; wings share the same fryer.

name: Jeremiah's Tavern
what: A tavern at 1104 Monroe Avenue in Rochester, the first of four rooms, frying wings that arrive "fresh, never frozen" in sauces the company mixes daily at its own commissary. The house claims a run of readers'-poll wins for wings longer than most of its staff have been alive. The Monroe Avenue kitchen also sells a plate, which is what Rochester calls the pile of meat and starch Nick Tahou Hots trademarked as the Garbage Plate.

name: J.R. Crickets
what: A Midtown Atlanta wing bar open since 1982, founded by Paul Juliano, who still runs it. Its lemon pepper wet — medium wing sauce with dry lemon pepper shaken over the top — is the wing a television episode made famous, under a name the kitchen did not give it. The house line is “Chicken Is Chicken, but the Wing Is the Thing!”

name: La Nova Pizzeria
what: A pizzeria on West Ferry Street in Buffalo's west side, run by three generations of the Todaro family, whose barbecue wing is the local counter-argument to cayenne and butter. The wings went from the pizzeria's own counter into a wholesale plant that ships them frozen across the country. Buffalo argues about whether a barbecue wing counts; La Nova sells them by the billion and does not enter the argument.

name: Mammoser's Tavern & Restaurant
what: A neighbourhood tavern on South Buffalo Street in Hamburg, twelve miles south of the city, pouring eighteen microbrew drafts and frying a wing in a house sauce built on four kinds of pepper. Bon Appétit put it third in Western New York in 2018. Closed Sundays.

name: Nine-Eleven Tavern
what: A cash-only corner tavern in South Buffalo, established 1981, whose wings come out large and heavily sauced in a recipe its late owner kept to himself. Buffalo Rising gives the address as 9-11 Bloomfield Avenue; the mailing address is 11. Five days a week, no cards, no delivery.

name: Peppa's Jerk Chicken
what: A Jamaican takeout counter on Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn's Little Caribbean, run by Gavin Hussey, whose jerk chicken is dry-rubbed, washed with vinegar and charred black before it is hacked apart to order. It stays open to six in the morning. A house scotch-bonnet jerk sauce goes over the top on request.

name: Prince's Hot Chicken Shack
aliases: Prince's Hot Chicken|Prince's Hot Chicken South|BBQ Chicken Shack
what: The Nashville hot chicken shack, started by James Thornton Prince and run since 1980 by his great-niece André Prince Jeffries. Chicken — breast, thigh or wing — is marinated, floured, fried to order and painted with a cayenne paste, then served on white bread under pickle slices. Everybody else's hot chicken is measured against it.

name: Uncle Remus Saucy Fried Chicken
what: A West Side Chicago fried-chicken counter whose sauce is in its name. Gus W. Rickette Sr. and Mary F. Rickette started it in 1963 as the G & G Chicken Shack and renamed it Uncle Remus in 1969; their daughter Charmaine Rickette Alfred runs it now. The company calls itself "a Black-owned and women-led business with a rich history rooted in Chicago's West Side."

name: The Wing Cafe & Tap House
aliases: The Wing Cafe and Tap House|Wing Cafe
what: A wing bar on Roswell Road in east Cobb County, outside Atlanta, carrying thirty-five to forty sauces and marinades and thirty to fifty beers on tap. It opened as a Wild Wing Cafe and kept trading under its own name after the chain link ended.

name: Wingnutz
aliases: Wingnutz Bar & Grill|WingNutz Bar and Grill|Wingnutz Buffalo
what: A sports bar on Millersport Highway in Williamsville, run by Ed and Alicia Wrazen, whose wings ran for thirteen years out of a Knights of Columbus hall before they had a restaurant. A podcast episode in 2021 turned a local following into an international one. The wings are large, crisp and sauced in mixes the couple make themselves.

name: Wingstop
what: A fast-food chain built on one part of the bird. Antonio Swad and Bernadette Fiaschetti opened the first Wingstop in Garland, Texas in 1994 and franchised it from 1997; the company is headquartered in Dallas and counted 3,255 restaurants system-wide on 27 June 2026. Orders go in at a counter or through an app, cook after the order lands, and come out sauced by hand in a bowl. The dining rooms carry a 1930s and 1940s pre-jet aviation theme.

name: Yum's II Carry-Out
what: A Chinese carryout on 14th Street NW in Washington, open past two most nights, selling fried wings, fried rice and french fries with mumbo sauce over them. It is the first address on most D.C. carryout lists.

name: Adrian Miller
aliases: the Soul Food Scholar|Adrian E. Miller
what: Food writer and historian of African American cooking, based in Denver. He describes himself as "a two-time James Beard Award-winning culinary author, professional speaker, certified barbecue judge, and recovering attorney based in Denver, Colorado." His books are where the fried chicken counter and the barbecue pit get written up as history rather than as colour.

name: Al Morganti
what: Philadelphia hockey writer and broadcaster, born 28 May 1953, and the man Wing Bowl is credited to. He covered the Flyers for the Philadelphia Inquirer from 1979 to 1989, analysed the NHL for ESPN from 1993 to 2005, and sat on WIP's morning show from 1993 to 2023, where he judged the eating stunts that got competitors into the contest.

name: André Prince Jeffries
what: Took over her great-uncle Thornton Prince's café in 1980, dropped the BBQ out of its name, and has run Prince's Hot Chicken Shack since. Her account of the dish is the account most writers work from, and she gives it without claiming to have settled it.

name: Angelo Cataldi
what: Philadelphia sports-radio morning host, born 13 March 1951, whose WIP show founded Wing Bowl in 1993 and ran it for twenty-six years. A newspaperman first: Providence Journal from 1977, Philadelphia Inquirer sports from 1983, a Pulitzer finalist for covering the 1986 Eagles and Buddy Ryan.

name: Antonio Swad
what: Founded Wingstop in Garland, Texas in 1994 with Bernadette Fiaschetti, franchised it from 1997, and sold it in 2003 at ninety units. He had already built Pizza Patrón, started 1986, and sold that in 2017. The National Buffalo Wing Festival put him in its Hall of Flame in 2010.

name: Argia B. Collins
what: Chicago barbecue man who made and bottled Mumbo sauce, and whose trademark on the name later beat a Washington, D.C. company that had been selling a sauce called mumbo for years. Salon records him as born in 1926 in Indianola, Mississippi and dead in 2003.

name: Bill "El Wingador" Simmons
what: Five-time Wing Bowl champion, born 1 November 1961, and the contest's own house name — El Wingador, 6 foot 5 and 290 pounds at his peak. He put the nickname on a line of wing sauce, went into the Wing Bowl Hall of Fame in February 2006, and went to state prison in 2013 on a cocaine charge.

name: Bob Gibson
what: Decatur, Alabama barbecue man, 1888 to 1972, who dunked hickory-smoked chicken in a sauce of mayonnaise, vinegar and black pepper. That sauce is the whole of Alabama white, and the wing version comes straight off his chickens. He was six foot four and over three hundred pounds, which is where the Big came from.

name: Calvin Trillin
what: American journalist and food writer, born 5 December 1935 in Kansas City, Missouri. He joined The New Yorker in 1963 and wrote its "U.S. Journal" series from 1967 to 1982, a piece a month from somewhere in the country. One of those pieces, in 1980, took the Buffalo wing out of western New York.

name: Dominic Bellissimo
what: Son of Frank and Teressa Bellissimo, tending the Anchor Bar on the night the house dates its wings to, 4 March 1964. He later owned the bar and spent decades promoting it and the wing. He died in March 1991, aged 68.

name: Drew Cerza
what: Founded the National Buffalo Wing Festival in 2002 and runs it. A marketing man by trade, he took the idea from a film that invented a Buffalo wing festival that did not exist, and built the one that does.

name: Frank Bellissimo
what: Opened the Anchor Bar in Buffalo with his wife Teressa in 1935 and ran the front of the house. His account of the first wings turns on a delivery that went wrong. The city of Buffalo honoured him by proclamation in 1977 and named 29 July Chicken Wing Day. He died in October 1980, aged 84.

name: Harold Pierce
aliases: Harold P. Pierce|the Fried Chicken King
what: Founded Harold's Chicken Shack in Chicago on 22 June 1950 and built it into the South Side's fried chicken chain, where a wing dinner comes cut over fries and drowned in mild sauce. Born 11 August 1917 in Midway, Alabama; died 8 March 1988 in Kankakee, Illinois, of prostate cancer, aged 70.

name: Jim Disbrow
what: Figure skater, skating official and co-founder of Buffalo Wild Wings, born 9 July 1948 and dead of brain cancer on 16 October 2002, aged 54. He started the chain in 1982 because he could not find a Buffalo-style wing in Ohio.

name: Joey Chestnut
what: American competitive eater, born 25 November 1983 in Fulton County, Kentucky and raised in Vallejo, California. Major League Eating ranks him first in the world; he holds 55 world records across 55 disciplines and has won the Nathan's hot dog belt 18 times. Several of those records are wings, which is why a wing project has him.

name: John Young
aliases: John Mack Young|John Young's Wings 'n Things|King of Wings
what: Sold chicken wings whole and uncut — breaded, deep-fried, and coated in a tomato-based sauce he called mumbo, or mambo — from a restaurant on Buffalo's East Side in the 1960s. He said he was selling them years before the Anchor Bar put them on a menu, and he said so for the rest of his life. Born in Stockton, Alabama in 1934, he came to Buffalo in 1948 at thirteen, and he died in 1998.

name: Teressa Bellissimo
what: Cooked at the Anchor Bar in Buffalo, which she opened with her husband Frank in 1935 and lived above. The bar credits her with frying the first plate of Buffalo wings on 4 March 1964 and sending it out with celery and blue cheese. She died in her apartment over the bar in November 1985, aged 84.

name: Thornton Prince
aliases: Thornton James Prince|James Thornton Prince|Thornton Prince III
what: Nashville cook whose family café put cayenne paste on fried chicken and made a city's dish out of it. Born near Franklin, Tennessee in December 1892 — the day is unknown — and died 15 February 1960, aged 67, of a cerebral thrombosis, according to research by the historian Rachel Louise Martin reported by Fox News in 2023. His great-niece André Prince Jeffries took over the café in 1980 and still runs it.

name: Buffalo Wing Trail
what: A list of wing joints, published by Visit Buffalo Niagara, the region's tourism bureau. It launched in April 2018 with twelve stops and carried fourteen when read on 16 September 2026, spread from Getzville and Amherst down through the city to East Aurora, Hamburg and Orchard Park. The trail's own words for what is on it: "14 neighborhood pubs and tucked-away corner taverns." There is no ranking, no scoring and no judging — it is an itinerary, which is exactly what makes it useful evidence.

name: City of Buffalo
aliases: Buffalo, New York|City Hall, Niagara Square
what: The municipal government that put its name on the wing, and then put a day on the calendar. Buffalo was incorporated as a city in 1832, seven years after the Erie Canal chose it for a terminus. It runs on a strong mayor–council system from City Hall at Niagara Square, with nine Common Council districts. In 1977 it issued a proclamation honouring Anchor Bar co-owner Frank Bellissimo and declared 29 July Chicken Wing Day.

name: National Chicken Council
what: The trade association of the US chicken industry, and the keeper of the number every Super Bowl story quotes. Founded in Richmond, Virginia in 1954 as the National Broiler Council, moved to Washington in 1965, renamed in 1999. Its producer and processor members account for about 95 percent of the chickens raised in the United States. Each January it publishes the Chicken Wing Report, a projection of how many wings Americans will eat on Super Bowl weekend.

name: Southern Foodways Alliance
what: An archive that records what cooks say about their own work. The Southern Foodways Alliance is based at the University of Mississippi's Center for the Study of Southern Culture and, in its own words, "documents, studies, and explores the diverse food cultures of the changing American South." It collects oral histories, makes short documentary films, publishes and podcasts as Gravy, and holds an annual symposium. For a wing record, it is the difference between a claim about a kitchen and a transcript from one.

name: U.S. Poultry & Egg Association
what: The trade association that funds the research and runs the equipment show behind the bird. Poultry and egg dealers met in Louisville in March 1947 and founded the Southeastern Poultry & Egg Association; it took the name U.S. Poultry & Egg Association as its membership spread coast to coast, moved to Tucker, Georgia in 1993, and calls itself an "All Feather" association — broilers, turkeys, ducks, eggs, breeding stock and the firms that supply them. It runs the International Production & Processing Expo in Atlanta each January.

name: National Buffalo Wing Festival
aliases: Wing Fest|National Buffalo Chicken Wing Festival
what: A two-day wing festival held on Labor Day weekend at Sahlen Field, the minor-league ballpark in downtown Buffalo. Drew Cerza founded it in 2002. Vendors sell wings by the order, contests run all weekend — the US Chicken Wing Eating Championship on the Sunday since 2003, plus amateur sauce contests, a 5K, Miss Buffalo Wing and Bobbing for Wings — and a Hall of Flame inducts the people, families and restaurants that shaped the wing.

name: National Chicken Wing Day
what: A food day on 29 July, kept by bars, chains and marketing departments across the United States. It comes from one city and one piece of paper: in 1977 Buffalo issued a proclamation honouring Anchor Bar co-owner Frank Bellissimo and declared 29 July Chicken Wing Day. The word national was added later, by everyone else.

name: Super Bowl Sunday
what: The biggest wing day in the United States, and the second-biggest American eating day of any kind after Thanksgiving dinner. The National Football League's championship game has been played on a Sunday since 1967 and on the second Sunday in February since 2022. The National Chicken Council projected 1.48 billion wings eaten around Super Bowl LX, in a release dated 28 January 2026 — a trade association's estimate of its own industry's product, not a government count.

name: Wing Bowl
what: A competitive wing-eating contest run by a Philadelphia sports radio station on the Friday before the Super Bowl. Al Morganti and Angelo Cataldi of WIP started it in 1993, for a city whose football team kept not reaching the Super Bowl. Two eaters and 150 spectators in a hotel lobby the first year; crowds over 20,000 in an arena by the 2000s, at six in the morning, with a field of qualifiers, costumed entourages, and women called Wingettes escorting the eaters. WIP ended it in 2018. A Las Vegas edition ran on 7 February 2026.

name: all flats
aliases: all drums|all flats no drums|flats only
what: An order that refuses half the bird. A wing splits one-for-one into a drumette and a flat, so a kitchen filling an all-flats order has to sell the drumettes to somebody else — which is why the answer is often no, and why the places that say yes charge for it.
root: all + flats (plural of flat); an order-modifier phrase, mirrored by all drums

name: atomic
what: Top of a house heat ladder, and a word that only means something inside one bar's list. Wingstop's own description of its Atomic flavour is "It's the hottest we've got. Find out for yourself" — Spice Level 5, the end of its scale. An atomic at one counter can be milder than a hot at another, because nothing standardises the rungs.
root: Ancient Greek átomos 'uncuttable' → Latin atomus → English atom → atomic; the wing sense borrows the bomb's connotation from the mid-20th century, not the physics

name: boneless
what: Breast meat cut into pieces, floured and spiced, fried or baked, then sauced like a wing and sold under the wing's name. Wikipedia describes them as "essentially small pieces of skinless, boneless chicken breast that are coated in flour and spices, then fried or baked, like a chicken nugget", sometimes marketed as wyngz. Restaurants added them as raw wing prices rose and as some diners asked for a neater plate.
root: bone + -less, the Old English privative suffix; the menu sense attaches the adjective to 'wing' and then lets the noun drop, leaving 'boneless' standing alone

name: Buffalo
what: A city's name working as an adjective. Buffalo now modifies a sauce rather than a place: vinegar-based cayenne hot sauce cut with melted butter, and anything wearing it. The word travelled further than the bird it started on — it has been applied to boneless wings made from breast, to chicken fries, nuggets and popcorn chicken, to shrimp, to cauliflower, to dip and to pizza.
root: Buffalo, New York (the city) → attributive adjective meaning 'dressed in cayenne hot sauce and melted butter'; the city takes its name from Buffalo Creek, whose own name is disputed

name: drumette
what: Upper of the three wing segments, and the meatiest. One bone, meat bunched at one end, skin all round: it eats like a small drumstick, which is where the name comes from. White meat, same as the breast. Two per bird.
root: drum (the drumstick it resembles) + -ette, the French diminutive that English borrowed for small versions of things

name: extra crispy
what: An order for more time in the oil. Not a flavour, not an upcharge in most places: a request that the wing stay down until the skin goes hard and the colour goes past golden. Kitchens read it as a range, which is why the same words get you different wings at two counters a block apart.
root: extra (Latin extra 'outside, beyond') + crispy (Old English crisp, from Latin crispus 'curled', re-pointed in English to mean brittle) — an intensifier stuck to a texture word

name: flapper
what: Cook's name for the wing tip: the pointed third segment, the one that carried the flight feathers. Skin and cartilage over two thin bones. It is the piece that gets thrown in the stock bucket, which is why most people who eat wings weekly have never heard the word.
root: flap (verb) + -er, the agent suffix — the part that does the flapping; pointer is built the same way off point

name: flat
what: Middle segment, two bones with a gap between them, and more skin per bite than any other piece of a chicken. Flat because it is — it lies down in the fryer basket and comes out on one plane. Two per bird.
root: the adjective flat, turned into a noun for the piece it describes; the competing name wingette is wing + -ette, the same diminutive that built drumette

name: hot honey
what: Honey infused with chillies, and the two-word name that turned it into a menu category. On wings it is a finish rather than a toss: drizzled over crust after the sauce, or whisked into a sauce to sweeten and thicken it. It reaches wings by way of pizza and fried chicken, where it landed first.
root: hot (chile-hot, not temperature-hot) + honey; an English compound that names the two ingredients and nothing else

name: mild sauce
what: Chicago's word for a red-brown condiment poured over fried chicken and fries at South and West Side chicken shacks and barbecue counters, and particularly associated with Black communities in Chicago. The sauce sits near barbecue sauce and near mumbo sauce; recipes vary substantially, and many formulations combine ketchup, barbecue sauce and hot sauce.
root: mild + sauce; a heat word that stopped being a heat word and became the name of a specific thing

name: mumbo
what: A word for a sweet-sour-hot red condiment, sold behind plexiglass in Washington carryouts and poured on fried wings, french fries, jumbo shrimp and fried rice. Barbecue-adjacent, sweeter than barbecue sauce, and by most accounts sourer or hotter as well; the recipe varies by counter.
root: no agreed etymon. As a commercial name the chain runs Argia B. Collins Sr.'s Chicago barbecue sauce → the registered mark MUMBO → the D.C. carryout word; the D.C. spelling mambo may be reshaping by the dance name

name: naked
what: Unbreaded. A wing fried in nothing but its own skin, no flour, no batter, no dredge. Hooters, which breads by hand as its original style, lists the alternative as Naked Wings and describes them: "Traditional style. No breading, but just as good. Order them with your favorite Hooters wing sauce or rub."
root: Old English nacod 'bare, unclothed' → Middle English naked; the menu sense is a metaphor, breading read as clothing

name: party wing
what: A supermarket's name for wings already broken down: tips off, joint cut, drumettes and flats loose in one bag or tray. The work a bar's prep cook does, done at the plant. The word says nothing about seasoning and nothing about size — it says only that you will not be cutting anything.
root: party + wing; retail compound, on the pattern of party pack and party size, where party means quantity-for-sharing rather than any occasion

name: weck
what: Half of a sandwich name that lost its other half. Weck is the kummelweck roll: kosher salt and caraway seeds baked onto the top, softer and fluffier than the German Kümmelbrötchen it descends from. Buffalo-area bakeries are the only commercial source for it. Beef on weck — rare roast beef, hand-carved thin, the top of the roll dipped in jus, horseradish spread to taste — is one of the three foods Buffalo is known for, with wings and sponge candy.
root: German Weck 'bread roll' (the word of the southwestern dialects — Palatinate, Saarland, Baden, Swabia; northern Germans say Brötchen) ← Old High German wecki, weggi 'wedge; wedge-shaped baked good' ← Proto-West Germanic *wagi ← Proto-Germanic *wagjaz 'wedge'. The full compound is kummelweck: German Kümmel 'caraway' (← Middle High German kümel, kumel ← Old High German kumil ← Proto-West Germanic *kumil 'caraway, cumin seed') + Weck. So the name means, exactly, caraway roll — and the bread is a wedge before it is a roll.

name: wet and dry
what: A two-way choice about the finish, asked after you have picked a flavour. Dry means the cooked wing gets tossed in seasoning — powder on crust. Wet means it gets tossed in something liquid, so butter or sauce carries the same seasoning. Same flavour name, two different foods.
root: wet + dry, plain antonyms recruited as a pair of menu terms: wet = finished in a liquid sauce, dry = finished in a powder

name: wing night
what: A weekly price special on wings, usually sold by the piece and usually paired with a drink minimum. The deal is the draw; the pitcher is the margin.
root: wing + night, on the pattern of ladies' night, trivia night, open-mic night — a weekday plus the thing that fills it

name: wing tip
what: Third segment, the pointed end. Skin, cartilage, two slivers of bone, almost no meat. Usually cut off before the wing reaches a fryer and boiled into stock instead, though some restaurants serve it still joined to the flat.
root: wing + tip, a plain compound; the piece also answers to flapper and to pointer, and all three names describe the same shape from a different angle

name: wing
what: A chicken's wing, and the pieces it becomes. Off the bird it runs drumette, flat and tip; a kitchen cuts it at both joints and usually throws the tip into stock, so what a menu calls a wing is one of two pieces. Order twenty and twenty pieces arrive, roughly ten birds' worth of one wing each.
root: Old Norse vængr → Middle English weng, winge → English wing; the food sense is a straight transfer from the bird's limb

name: Buffalo murals
what: Buffalo paints its own story on its walls, and the wing is part of what gets painted. The city's public art runs from commissioned murals on Main Street and Hertel Avenue to neighbourhood walls raised by crowdfunding, and at least one of them exists to settle an argument: in November 2021 a mural went up at Jefferson and Carlton, on the corner where John Young's Wings 'n Things stood, recreating the artwork that had hung inside his shop. The murals are copyrighted by the people who painted them, and one Buffalo muralist has invoiced businesses for using images of his wall, which is why this page names walls and does not reproduce them.

name: Chicken shack signs
what: The sign over a wing or fried-chicken counter is a working document. It has to be readable from a car at thirty miles an hour, name the shop, say CHICKEN, and usually price something. It comes in two families that overlap: brush-lettered paint, on plywood, on stucco, on the window glass itself; and the internally lit plastic box with changeable letters underneath. The cartoon bird is optional and very common. Almost none of it is signed, almost all of it is made locally, and it is replaced rather than restored, which is why the record of it is photographic.

name: Hot sauce labels
aliases: hot sauce bottle art|pepper sauce labels
what: A hot sauce label sells one thing before it sells any other: how much it will hurt. The genre has a settled vocabulary — devils, flames, skulls, warning text set like a hazard placard, a name that is a dare, and often a number. Beneath the artwork the same panel carries what federal law requires, including an ingredient list in descending order by weight, which is why this site can read a bottle's ingredient rank off a photograph of its back. The front is a promise. The back is a fact.

name: Neon chicken
what: A chicken drawn in bent glass tube, filled with gas, and run off a transformer over a bar, a drive-in or a wing counter. The bird is usually animated in the cheap way neon animates: two or three sets of tubes switched in sequence so a wing flaps, steam rises, or an arrow chases. Neon signs are made by hand, by a bender working a ribbon burner, which is why a town's neon looks like the shops of the two or three benders who worked there. They are expensive to build, expensive to repair, and the first thing an owner replaces when a tube goes, which is why the surviving ones are mostly in cities that decided to protect them.

name: Rooster weathervanes
what: A rooster cut or moulded in sheet metal, balanced on a spindle, and put on a roof to show which way the wind blows. It is the oldest American use of a chicken as a public sign, it predates every wing counter by centuries, and the shape it settled into — flat body, raised comb, fanned tail, one leg forward — is the same silhouette a fried chicken sign draws today. American vanes were made in copper and zinc by nineteenth-century firms working from moulds, and museums now hold them as folk sculpture; the Smithsonian American Art Museum has released photographs of several under CC0.

name: Wing festival posters
aliases: Wing Fest poster art|wing contest promotional art
what: A wing festival poster does four things at once: names the event, fixes the date and the gate, lists the sponsors in descending size, and supplies a mascot the event can print on a T-shirt. The National Buffalo Wing Festival, founded in Buffalo in 2002 and held on Labor Day weekend, is the genre's anchor; Philadelphia's Wing Bowl, run by a radio station from 1993 to 2018, produced the same artwork in a louder register. The art is commercial, it is dated by design, and almost none of it is free to reuse — which is why this page describes it rather than shows it.

name: Boneless is not a wing
aliases: Berkheimer v. REKM|The boneless wing case
what: On 25 July 2024 the Supreme Court of Ohio held, 4 to 3, that a diner who swallowed a chicken bone from a boneless wing could not take his negligence claim to a jury, because he could reasonably have guarded against it. The case is Berkheimer v. REKM, L.L.C., 2024-Ohio-2787, 177 Ohio St.3d 431, docket 2023-0293. The majority wrote that calling the item a boneless wing described a cooking style. The dissent called that reasoning jabberwocky, twice. The argument the case dropped into is older than the case and older than the menu category: a boneless wing is breast meat, battered and fried, and the federal standard that governs what may be labelled a wing does not cover a restaurant menu at all.

name: Free to use
aliases: Sources and licences|What this project stands on
what: Every map, price, coordinate and recipe on this site comes from somewhere a reader can go and check. This page names each archive, dataset, directory and licence, says what it is good for, says what it will not tell you, and names the ones this project could not get into. Licences are quoted from the publisher's own terms. Dates are the dates I read them, which for all of these is 16 September 2026.

name: Ranch against blue cheese
what: Buffalo sends out blue cheese. America buys ranch. Blue cheese reached the wing plate on the first night of the Anchor Bar story, off the antipasto tray, and it is still the house cup along the city's wing trail. Ranch was invented by a plumbing contractor named Steve Henson in the early 1950s, sold by mail from a Santa Barbara County guest ranch from 1957, bought by Clorox in 1972, and has outsold every other salad dressing in the United States since 1992. Asked what they eat wings with, more Americans say ranch than say blue cheese, by roughly two to one in the trade association's own polling. Both numbers and both dips are set out below, with whose figures they are and when they were taken.

name: The flat and the drum
what: A chicken wing has three joints and yields two pieces a kitchen will sell: the drumette, which is the humerus with the meat pushed to one end, and the flat, which is the two-boned middle section carrying most of the skin. The tip goes to stock. One bird gives one of each per wing, in a fixed ratio nobody can change, which is the whole economics of the argument: a counter can let you order all flats, but it cannot buy a bird that grows two of them. Federal regulation names the drumette and declines to name the flat. Survey respondents prefer the drum by a wide margin and split sharply by who is answering. No public price series prices one piece against the other.

name: The origin fight
what: Two Buffalo kitchens claim the wing, and neither claim rests on a document. The Anchor Bar dates the dish to the night of 4 March 1964 and tells the story three different ways. John Young was selling breaded whole wings in a tomato sauce he called mumbo from 1961, registered his shop's name at the county courthouse, and said the Anchor Bar carried no wings as a regular menu item until 1974. A 1969 newspaper profile of the Anchor Bar does not mention wings. Duff's started selling them across town that same year. The city proclaimed a Chicken Wing Day in 1977, Calvin Trillin carried the story out of western New York in 1980, and the National Buffalo Wing Festival put John Young in its Hall of Flame in 2013. This page lays out who claims what and on what evidence.

name: The price of a wing
what: In 1964 the wing was the cheapest thing on the bird, which is the premise every origin story rests on. In the week of 7 to 11 September 2026 it traded wholesale at 110.02 cents a pound, twice the price of a drumstick and ten times the price of the backs and necks that the Anchor Bar story says were supposed to arrive instead. It has been dearer than that: 325 cents a pound in May 2021, when cold storage ran to its lowest level since 2012. Every figure on this page carries its date and whose figure it is, and the ones I could not get are named too.
